title: The Science of Sleep: Why Your Brain Needs 8 Hours

slides.heading: The Science of Sleep
slides.body: Why Your Brain Desperately Needs 8 Hours Every Night

slides.heading: Sleep Is Not Passive Rest
slides.body: Your brain is intensely active while you sleep. It cycles through distinct stages — light sleep, deep sleep, and REM — each performing critical maintenance tasks that waking life simply cannot provide.

slides.heading: The Brain's Nightly Cleanup Crew
slides.body: During deep sleep, the glymphatic system flushes toxic waste proteins from your brain — including amyloid-beta, a key culprit in Alzheimer's disease. Missing sleep means skipping this essential detox.

slides.heading: Memory Gets Consolidated Overnight
slides.body: REM sleep is when your brain replays and strengthens new memories, transferring them from short-term to long-term storage. Studying then sleeping beats cramming all night — every single time.

slides.heading: Sleep Deprivation Impairs Like Alcohol
slides.body: After 17–19 hours awake, your cognitive performance matches someone with a blood alcohol level of 0.05%. After 24 hours, it equals being legally drunk. Yet most people don't feel how impaired they are.

slides.heading: Your Hormones Reset While You Sleep
slides.body: Growth hormone peaks during deep sleep — essential for muscle repair and cell renewal at any age. Cortisol (stress hormone) drops, and leptin/ghrelin (hunger hormones) rebalance. Chronic short sleep drives overeating.

slides.heading: The Immune System Depends on Sleep
slides.body: Sleep triggers production of cytokines — proteins that fight infection and inflammation. People sleeping under 6 hours are 4× more likely to catch a cold when exposed to a virus compared to those getting 8 hours.

slides.heading: Why 8 Hours Is the Magic Number
slides.body: Most adults need 7–9 hours to complete 4–5 full sleep cycles. Only about 1–3% of people are true "short sleepers" due to a rare gene variant. Feeling fine on 6 hours is usually just adaptation — not immunity.

slides.heading: Small Habits That Unlock Better Sleep
slides.body: Keep a consistent bedtime, even on weekends. Avoid screens 1 hour before bed (blue light suppresses melatonin). Keep your bedroom cool (65–68°F). These three changes can dramatically improve sleep quality.

slides.heading: Sleep Is a Superpower
slides.body: Protect your sleep like you protect your health — because they are the same thing. Every hour you invest in sleep pays dividends in focus, mood, immunity, and longevity.
